analysis.one_liner: Designates millions of acres of Northern Rockies public land as wilderness, off-limits to logging, mining, and drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would designate federal land in Idaho, Montana, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming as wilderness, wild and scenic rivers, wildlife corridors, and recovery areas. Once designated, those lands could not have new roads, logging, mining, or oil and gas drilling without another act of Congress. It was introduced in February 2015, referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then a subcommittee, and never got any further.
analysis.who_benefits: Hikers, hunters, anglers, and backcountry users get permanent access to undeveloped public land; downstream towns and farms keep cleaner water from protected headwaters; and companies that do land-restoration work would get contracts under the bill's recovery program. The bill's findings argue the land is worth more left intact than as timber.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Backcountry users, anglers, hunters, and restoration contractors

how_it_helps.text: Designates wilderness, wild and scenic rivers, wildlife corridors, and wildland recovery areas across five Northern Rockies states [S2].
Bars new road construction, timber harvest, mining, and oil and gas leasing on the covered roadless lands without a future act of Congress [S2].

The bill's findings state that the protected headwaters feed the Columbia, Snake, Missouri, and other river systems used by farms, ranches, and municipal water supplies, and that protection would lower water treatment costs [S3].
The bill would create restoration jobs on damaged federal land, with contracts for local businesses, and cites below-cost timber sales as a drain on taxpayers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Timber, mining, and oil and gas companies lose access to the designated federal lands, and the rural communities built around those industries would bear the adjustment. Snowmobile and off-road-vehicle users lose the areas designated as wilderness, since wilderness bans motorized travel.
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber, mining, and oil and gas interests; motorized recreation users

drawbacks.text: Wilderness designation bans motorized recreation, so snowmobilers and off-road-vehicle riders lose access to areas they currently use; the bill's own definition of development makes no carve-out for them [S3].

Restricting logging, mining, and drilling removes the work those industries support in rural Northern Rockies towns; the bill responds with restoration jobs but does not claim those fully replace extractive employment [S3].

The bill imposed designations across entire ecosystems by national statute rather than through locally negotiated land deals, and its sponsor and nearly all of its 37 cosponsors represented states outside the region [S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a large, permanent public good — millions of acres of roadless land, clean river headwaters, and wildlife habitat — at the direct expense of extractive industries and some recreation access. Its weakness was process, not design: it was written as a blanket national mandate for five states whose own representatives were not on board, which is precisely why it could not move. An honest supporter would concede that the restoration jobs it promises would not come close to replacing logging and mining work in the short term.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, then to its Federal Lands subcommittee, and neither ever took it up; when the Congress ended in January 2017, it died without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Carolyn Maloney introduced the bill on February 13, 2015 with 30 original cosponsors, all but one a Democrat [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the day it was introduced [S5].
On March 16, 2015 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Federal Lands, which is where the record ends [S5].
The bill gathered 37 cosponsors — 36 Democrats and 1 Republican — but never received a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or any action in the Senate [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, timber, mining, and oil and gas companies kept their access to the roadless federal lands, and the region's management continued under existing forest plans. The public gained nothing from the bill's death; it simply kept the status quo that the bill was written to change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Extractive industries that would have been restricted

sides.party_line_note: 37 of the bill's 38 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; the one Republican was Walter Jones of North Carolina, and no member from the five affected states led the bill [S4].

industries.note: The bill barred timber harvest and new road construction on the covered roadless lands without a future act of Congress. The bill's findings counter that federal timber sales in the region run below cost and cost taxpayers money.

industries.industry: Mining and oil and gas companies
industries.note: The bill prohibited oil and gas leasing, mining, and other development that would impair the roadless character of the covered lands. Those leases and claims would have been off the table permanently.

industries.industry: Motorized recreation (snowmobile and off-road vehicle users)
industries.note: Wilderness designation bans motorized travel, so these users would lose access to large areas they can reach today. They are ordinary users of public land whose access is traded away for conservation.

industries.industry: Hunting, fishing, and wilderness-based recreation businesses
industries.note: The bill's findings say intact roadless lands support sustainable economies through hunting, fishing, and wilderness recreation, and that outfitting and tourism depend on the scenery and fisheries the designation would protect.
The bill would fund wildland recovery work on damaged federal tracts, creating contracts for local businesses doing restoration work.
